extracted.intended_audience: general readers and fans of comedy interested in controversial/dark humor (WatchMojo audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A pop-culture listicle ranking Frankie Boyle's most brutal/controversial jokes, highlighting features that make his material shocking, boundary-pushing, or politically charged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controversy / Provocativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The joke is a 'controversial moment' or 'to-the-bone' line that provokes public debate or strong reactions; the easily offended should look away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page frames picks as 'most controversial moments' and opens with 'The easily offended should look away now.' Examples: Harvey Price joke prompting a high-profile feud and censorship debate; jokes widely covered by newspapers/broadcasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taboo Subject Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Material addresses taboo or sensitive topics (HIV, disability, depression, suicide, child abuse, etc.), using those subjects as the core of the gag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited include jokes about 'Coping with HIV', disability (Harvey Price), depression/suicide (Robin Williams), politicians and child abuse, and Michael Jackson's children's hospital. The page notes these topics are 'no laughing matter' yet Boyle 'pushes the boundaries'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary-Pushing / Crossing the Line
rubrics_metrics.description: The comedian deliberately pushes or crosses conventional lines of acceptability; if there is a line, Boyle has crossed it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as 'ploughs on regardless', 'pushes the boundaries of what's acceptable, then pushes them a little further', and 'decimates all remaining boundaries.' Used to justify placing highest-ranked material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shock Value / Audience Reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: The joke elicits visible shock from the audience (silence, shocked faces) and relies on that reaction as a marker of its brutality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page remarks that 'the shocked faces in the audience tell you everything you need to know' and notes speechless reactions on 'Mock the Week' and awkward silence in shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting Public Figures / Celebrities
rubrics_metrics.description: Material singles out TV personalities, celebrities, sports figures or politicians (Katie Price, John Terry, members of Royal Family, Nigel Farage) as the subject of attack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boyle 'rarely has any qualms over offending TV personalities' and several entries revolve around famous targets; such targets sometimes trigger feuds or press backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roasting / Direct Personal Insults
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes that directly insult or 'hot-seat' individuals in the audience or public, dismantling physical appearance or personal traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as 'hot-seats a couple of audience members, and ruthlessly dismantles their physical appearances' and includes put-downs like 'your mum' jokes; no heckle will save you from Boyle's wrath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political / Social Commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes that have an underlying political or social point — critiquing charities, politicians, institutions, or societal hypocrisy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include dismantling the idea of charity (Comic Relief, aid organisations), routines about politicians and alleged child abuse, and critiques of the Royal Family or UKIP. Page notes 'there is often a political point lurking behind the jokes he makes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody and Accent/Impersonation
rubrics_metrics.description: Using parody, accent change, or impersonation to build a rant or character that escalates into brutal material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: parodying Nigel Farage and 'the good old days' by changing accent and progressively worsening the past; parody functions as a comedic device to amplify outrage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-up to a Dark Punchline (Structural Craft)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a measured set-up that leads into a particularly 'messed up' anecdote or fiercest attack; structural build-up is part of the joke's potency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page notes that a seemingly ordinary set-up ('that's just the set-up for Frankie’s fiercest attack') leads to unexpectedly brutal payoffs, suggesting craftsmanship in timing and escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roleplay / Character Adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming a dark or demonic persona/voice to deliver the joke (role-based performance that intensifies the gag).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Assuming a demonic role and reinterpreting the words of Michael Jackson' for his darkest joke; role adoption heightens shock and distance/permission to say taboo things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demolition of Stereotypes / Satirical Exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Using harsh humor to expose or demolish stereotypes, patronising attitudes, or institutional hypocrisy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: dissecting patronising charity drives and gap year volunteers, 'demolishing many a stereotype' while making a political point; satire serves argument as well as offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media Impact / Controversy Aftermath
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which a joke provokes press coverage, public debate, censorship discussions, or formal fallout (feuds, broadcasting attention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Harvey Price joke 'triggered a censorship debate' and received 'unprecedented coverage' — media reaction is used as a signifier of a joke's brutality and cultural impact.
